newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Letter bomb addressed to Arabic paper found at U.N..
newsitem.headline: Letter bomb addressed to Arabic paper found at U.N..

text.p: A letter bomb addressed to the U.N. bureau of the Arabic-language newspaper Al-Hayat was found in a messenger room at U.N. headquarters on Monday and later safely detonated, a U.N. spokesman said.

The device was discovered a few hours after a letter bomb exploded at the same newspaper's London office, wounding two security guards. Four more suspect devices were found there later, British police said.
U.N. security evacuated and closed off parts of two floors of the 38-storey U.N. complex and the New York police bomb squad was called in.

U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said the bomb was in a white greeting-card sized enveloped addressed to Al-Hayat -- similar to several devices mailed earlier this month to the same Saudi Arabian-owned newspaper's Washington bureau.
"It was a live bomb and it was detonated (under controlled conditions) in the (basement) garage," he said.
Only one bomb was found though a second piece of mail was earlier treated as a suspicious object.
Secretary-General Kofi Annan issued a statement calling the incident "a reminder of the dangerous conditions under which many journalists must work."

"The secretary-general unreservedly condemns this cowardly act which is an assault on the United Nations itself and on the principle of free expression for which the United Nations stands," the statement added.

The bomb, of a type which explodes when the envelope is opened, had not been detected in the basement area where mail is first sorted but after it reached a messenger station on the second floor, Eckhard said.
It was addressed to the newspaper's bureau rather than to any specific individual.
The evacuation of part of the press area resulted in a 90-minute delay in the U.N. spokesman's daily news conference.

A U.N. source said mail delivered to the United Nations was normally scanned as a security precaution. The precautions were stepped up after Al-Hayat's U.N. correspondent, Raghida Dergham, informed U.N. security of the London incident.
"We at Al-Hayat do not have any particular suspect," Dergham said. "We are going to go on with our very independent reporting," she added.

The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation launched an international investigation earlier this month after eight letter bombs made to look like Christmas cards were mailed from Egypt to the United States.
Four arrived at Al-Hayat's Washington office and a fifth was found in the mail system. Three other devices turned up in the area around Leavenworth federal prison in Kansas.

The FBI has dismissed as "speculative" reports it is investigating a possible connection between the letter bombs and the 1993 bombing of the World Trade Centre and a foiled plot to bomb other New York landmarks.

Mohammad Salameh, a militant Moslem jailed for life for the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing, is in Leavenworth, as are Victor Alvarez and Mohammed Saleh who were convicted of plotting to blow up U.N. headquarters and other New York targets.
